items.title: Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20
items.summary:
Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20 years of HN to 6,454 videos that keep being recommended. *Significantly* better viewing experience, ~2 hours with Opus 5.5:
https://t.co/JIhXN7OSh1

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

items.summary: As AI systems become more capable, researchers are increasingly asking a practical question: Can AI do more than help write code for computing systems? Specifically, can it actively participate in the design of complex computing systems and rapidly translate algorithms into silicon? New work in AI-driven chip design suggests the answer is yes. But a promising algorithm is only the beginning of a hardware design. Turning it into an efficient chip requires exploring how to organize computation, [...] AI for chip design connects two forms of progress into a reciprocal relationship: Better hardware enables more capable AI, and more capable AI can help engineers develop better hardware. Cost-efficient agent factories make that relationship more practical. By making each search more affordable, open models and distributed inference create room to test more ideas and, with better search strategies, turn that opportunity into better chips. It also depends on how much verified exploration an organization can afford. Model capability, the assignment of agent roles, and the infrastructure serving those models all shape the hardware improvements that are attainable within a real engineering budget. items.title: AI Designs Computer Chips We Can't Understand — But They Seem to Work Really Well
items.summary:
## AI at the helm

The AI-driven method focused on designing wireless chips, a type of computer chips used for high-frequency applications like 5G networks, radar systems, and advanced sensing technologies. These circuits power innovations in everything from radar systems to autonomous vehicles but their development is notoriously slow. Engineers would start on predefined templates and manually optimize or improve designs through iterative simulations and testing. [...] A A

Edited and reviewed by Zoe Gordon

The AI design features unusual and efficient, circuitry patterns. Credit: Emir Ali Karahan, Princeton University.

Engineers usually design wireless chips using familiar patterns and templates, refining them through simulations and painstaking testing. But a series of studies is proposing a different approach: a deep-learning-enabled design process for creating circuits and components. [...] In May 2025, the National Semiconductor Technology Center announced a nearly $10 million award for a Princeton-led effort to develop AI-powered design tools for wireless chips. The programme brought together researchers and industry partners, with Sengupta directing the research.

But just a few months later, the project received a stop-work order.

According to Friar, the growth was driven by OpenAI's frontier research and enterprise business.

"Our enterprise business doubled quarter over quarter," she explained, adding that OpenAI's revenue is now split 50/50 between its enterprise and consumer business.

"What's driving that is products like Coding, Cyber, starting to get more virtual assistants like Dots into the enterprise," Friar said. [...] Friar also said that OpenAI's consumer business is continuing to grow, with sales improving 20% quarter over quarter and subscriptions topping 100 million users. The company has 1.2 billion weekly active users.

OpenAI rival Anthropic (ANTH.PVT) kicked off its roadshow on Tuesday ahead of its planned initial public offering, which could take place Nov. 19 or Nov. 20.

Anthropic's own enterprise efforts have been a boon for its bottom line. [...] Dots is OpenAI's AI agent platform for enterprise.

The company's small- and medium-business offering also grew more in the third quarter than in the prior six quarters, she added.
